blocks.text: A set answers a membership question. It intentionally forgets how many times an equivalent value arrived unless that information is stored separately. Constructing a set from identifiers one, two, two, and four yields three members. blocks.text: Equivalence deserves explicit attention for domain keys. An ordered set treats two keys as equivalent when neither compares before the other under its comparator. A case-insensitive identifier policy might therefore consider two differently cased strings the same key. The stored spelling may still be one of the original representations, so output policy must be decided separately from identity policy.

blocks.text: The ordering relation must behave consistently. It should not change because a mutable global flag switches modes during a lookup. Nor should a comparator use an external table that can change while keys remain stored. The tree or other ordered structure was organized under earlier comparisons, and a changed relation can invalidate that organization without moving a single node.

blocks.text: Canonicalization is one way to make identity explicit. For an ASCII-only exercise, validate the permitted characters and convert letters according to a fixed rule before inserting. Do not casually call that general Unicode normalization; text identity across languages has additional rules. A precise narrow grammar is more reliable than a broad unsupported claim.

blocks.text: The standard set-operation algorithms operate on sorted ranges under a compatible comparator, not on arbitrary unsorted containers. Their merge-like traversal advances through the ranges without searching each key from scratch. For input lengths n and m, the work is linear in their combined traversal size under the comparison model. Multiset inputs have multiplicity semantics that differ from simply deduplicating everything first.

blocks.text: Set operations are useful descriptions of real reconciliation tasks. Let required contain machines scheduled for maintenance and completed contain machines reporting success. required - completed identifies outstanding machines. completed - required identifies unexpected reports. Their intersection identifies scheduled machines that completed. Their union identifies every machine mentioned by either source.

blocks.text: The standard set algorithms work by coordinated traversal of sorted ranges. If the left current value is smaller, it cannot match a later smaller value on the right because the right range is ordered. This allows one side to advance without restarting a search. The linear combined-traversal bound comes from each iterator moving forward at most through its input length.

blocks.text: Multiplicity changes the interpretation. On sorted ranges containing duplicates, standard set operations have specified multiset-style counts rather than an automatic “deduplicate everything” rule. A union can preserve the greater multiplicity of equivalent elements; an intersection can preserve the smaller. When the application truly wants membership, build unique inputs or explicitly deduplicate first.

blocks.text: Deterministic output should be an explicit layer. blocks.text: “Deterministic” also needs a tie and formatting policy. A reproducible report might sort by descending count and then ascending category name. That rule should be tested with equal counts, not only distinct ones.

blocks.text: Key cost changes the comparison. An ordered lookup can perform several comparisons, each potentially inspecting a string prefix. A hashed lookup computes a hash over the key and then may compare colliding candidates. Long shared prefixes, expensive normalization, and repeated hashing can dominate container overhead. Complexity labels about the number of key operations do not remove the cost of those operations.

Next write a category counter with checked increments and a nonmutating query function. Verify that asking for a missing category leaves the number of entries unchanged. Decide whether the query returns optional count or zero, and explain why either can be appropriate only under its documented meaning.

Build a report sorted by descending count and then ascending category. Use a fixture with at least two equal counts. Generate several permutations of the same input tokens and verify identical reports. This tests that ingestion order does not accidentally determine presentation order when the contract says it should not.

For a design exercise, add a range query such as identifiers between two lexical boundaries. Explain how this changes the relative convenience of ordered and hash-based representations. Do not conclude from a single extra operation that all hash tables should be replaced; consider its frequency and the full workload.
Acceptance evidence. Record the identity policy, duplicate policy, missing-query behavior, report order, and numeric limit. Retain a regression showing that a read-only query does not mutate state.

Review reasoning. Why does a set lose frequency information? It stores membership under an equivalence rule. Why is difference directional? It asks which left-side members are absent on the right. Why can two maps be equal while their iteration orders differ? Mapping semantics and traversal policy are separate. Why test equal-count reports? They expose an unspecified tie rule. Why must equality and ordering remain stable while keys are stored? The representation’s organization depends on those decisions.
